  - title: 'Army Quote of the Day from Alexander the Great: ‘I am not afraid of an army
      of lions led by a sheep; I am afraid of…’'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/army-quote-of-the-day-from-alexander-the-great-i-am-not-afraid-of-an-army-of-lions-led-by-a-sheep-i-am-afraid-of/
    text: 'Alexander III of Macedon—Alexander the Great—stands as a case study in how
      leadership can transform military power. Born in Pella and educated under Aristotle,
      he became regent as a teenager and took the throne at 20 after Philip II’s assassination.
      He then launched a blistering campaign across Asia Minor, the Levant, Egypt, Babylonia,
      and Persia, ultimately pushing toward India—remaining undefeated in battle. By
      30, he had forged a vast empire, but he died suddenly two years later in Babylon
      after a night of wine and a swift fever. The post Army Quote of the Day from Alexander
      the Great: ‘I am not afraid of an army of lions led by a sheep; I am afraid of…’
      appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Alexander the Great, who became king at 20 after his father's
      assassination, transformed military power through his undefeated campaigns across
      Asia and the creation of a vast empire, before dying unexpectedly at 32.
    paragraph_summary: Alexander III of Macedon, known as Alexander the Great, exemplifies
      how effective leadership can enhance military strength. Born in Pella and trained
      by Aristotle, he became regent in his teens and ascended to the throne at 20 following
      the assassination of his father, Philip II. He embarked on an aggressive military
      campaign across Asia Minor, the Levant, Egypt, Babylonia, and Persia, achieving
      an undefeated record in battle and establishing a vast empire by the age of 30.
      However, his reign was cut short when he died unexpectedly in Babylon at 32 after
      a night of drinking and a sudden illness.
    published: '2026-01-19T12:29:02+00:00'

  - title: 'YF-118G: The Bird of Prey Stealth Aircraft Has a Message for the Air Force'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/yf-118g-the-bird-of-prey-stealth-aircraft-has-a-message-for-the-air-force/
    text: 'The YF-118G “Bird of Prey” was a privately funded Boeing (formerly McDonnell
      Douglas) Phantom Works technology demonstrator built to prove advanced stealth
      could be designed and manufactured faster and cheaper. Developed in secrecy at
      Area 51, it used a blended-wing-body shape, shielded intake, and gapless control
      surfaces to reduce radar signature, while single-piece composite construction
      minimized seams that reflect radar energy. The post YF-118G: The Bird of Prey
      Stealth Aircraft Has a Message for the Air Force appeared first on 19FortyFive
      .'
    one_sentence_summary: The YF-118G "Bird of Prey," a stealth technology demonstrator
      developed by Boeing at Area 51, showcased advanced design techniques for reducing
      radar signatures and manufacturing costs through its innovative blended-wing-body
      shape and composite construction.
    paragraph_summary: The YF-118G "Bird of Prey," a technology demonstrator developed
      by Boeing's Phantom Works, aimed to showcase the feasibility of creating advanced
      stealth aircraft more efficiently and cost-effectively. Built in secrecy at Area
      51, the aircraft featured a blended-wing-body design, shielded intakes, and gapless
      control surfaces to minimize its radar signature, while its single-piece composite
      construction reduced seams that could reflect radar energy. The article emphasizes
      the significance of the YF-118G's innovations for the future of stealth technology
      in the Air Force.
    published: '2026-01-19T12:20:35+00:00'

  - title: 32,000 Ton ‘Super’ Battleship USS Texas Has a Message for the Navy
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/32000-ton-super-battleship-uss-texas-has-a-message-for-the-navy/
    text: USS Texas, a 1914 New York-class battleship and one of the few preserved U.S.
      dreadnoughts, is nearing the end of a major restoration after decades as a museum
      ship left her hull badly degraded. Leaks, equipment failures, and a six-degree
      list helped spur a full move to Galveston’s Gulf Copper dry dock in 2022, where
      crews replaced hull plating, removed corrosion, reinforced structures, and overhauled
      long-neglected systems. The post 32,000 Ton ‘Super’ Battleship USS Texas Has a
      Message for the Navy appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The USS Texas, a historic 1914 battleship, is undergoing extensive
      restoration in Galveston after years of neglect left it with significant structural
      issues and degradation.
    paragraph_summary: The USS Texas, a historic 1914 New York-class battleship and
      one of the last preserved U.S. dreadnoughts, is undergoing a significant restoration
      after years of deterioration as a museum ship. The vessel, which suffered from
      leaks, equipment failures, and a notable six-degree list, was moved to Galveston's
      Gulf Copper dry dock in 2022 for extensive repairs. Crews have been working on
      replacing hull plating, removing corrosion, reinforcing structures, and overhauling
      neglected systems to restore the battleship to a more stable condition.
    published: '2026-01-19T12:11:11+00:00'

      rewards. Nuclear arming could lower the perceived threshold for nuclear use and

  - title: Boeing X-32 Stealth Fighter Has a Message for the U.S. Military
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/boeing-x-32-stealth-fighter-has-a-message-for-the-u-s-military/
    text: 'Boeing’s X-32 was built to win the Joint Strike Fighter contest with simplicity:
      fewer parts, cost-focused commonality, and a large one-piece delta wing designed
      for efficiency and hefty internal fuel. Test pilots praised its controllability—some
      likened carrier-approach handling to an F/A-18. The concept also helped seed sensor
      work that later informed the AN/APG-79 radar family. The post Boeing X-32 Stealth
      Fighter Has a Message for the U.S. Military appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Boeing's X-32, designed for the Joint Strike Fighter competition,
      emphasized simplicity and cost-effectiveness with its efficient delta wing and
      controllability, influencing future sensor technology like the AN/APG-79 radar.
    paragraph_summary: Boeing's X-32 was designed to compete in the Joint Strike Fighter
      contest by emphasizing simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and a large one-piece delta
      wing for improved efficiency and fuel capacity. Test pilots noted its excellent
      controllability, comparing its carrier approach handling to that of the F/A-18.
      Additionally, the X-32's design contributed to advancements in sensor technology,
      influencing the development of the AN/APG-79 radar family. The article highlights
      the X-32's legacy and its implications for the U.S. military's future aircraft
      development.
    published: '2026-01-19T00:15:10+00:00'

  - title: Why Making Iran “Pay” for Regime Change Would Backfire Fast
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/why-making-iran-pay-for-regime-change-would-backfire-fast/
    text: 'Donald Trump’s transactional instincts could tempt him to treat Iranian regime
      change like Ukraine or Venezuela: help, but only for a commercial payoff. That
      approach would be politically toxic inside Iran. Iranian collective memory is
      shaped by nineteenth-century “concessions” in which foreign powers extracted monopolies—rail,
      banking, tobacco, fisheries, and, most famously, oil. T The post Why Making Iran
      “Pay” for Regime Change Would Backfire Fast appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The article argues that Donald Trump's transactional approach
      to supporting regime change in Iran, akin to his strategies in Ukraine and Venezuela,
      could backfire politically due to Iran's historical resentment towards foreign
      exploitation and concessions.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the potential consequences of Donald Trump's
      transactional approach to Iranian regime change, likening it to his strategies
      in Ukraine and Venezuela, where assistance is contingent on commercial benefits.
      This mindset could be politically detrimental in Iran, where historical grievances
      stem from foreign powers exploiting the country through monopolistic concessions
      in various sectors, including oil. The piece argues that framing regime change
      as a pay-for-play scenario could provoke backlash and resistance from the Iranian
      populace, given their collective memory of exploitation.
    published: '2026-01-18T23:57:18+00:00'

  - title: How a 1,000-foot U.S. Navy Supercarrier Gets Scrapped for 1 Cent
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/how-a-1000-foot-u-s-navy-supercarrier-gets-scrapped-for-1-cent/
    text: 'USS John F. Kennedy (CV-67) has begun its final chapter, departing Philadelphia
      for Brownsville, Texas to be dismantled after museum plans failed to secure funding,
      berthing, and long-term upkeep. The move highlights why retired carriers are sold
      for one cent: towing, docking, hazardous-material handling, and regulated shipbreaking
      make them expensive liabilities despite their size and history. The post How a
      1,000-foot U.S. Navy Supercarrier Gets Scrapped for 1 Cent appeared first on 19FortyFive
      .'
    one_sentence_summary: The USS John F. Kennedy is en route to Brownsville, Texas
      for dismantling after failed museum plans, illustrating the high costs associated
      with decommissioning retired aircraft carriers, which are often sold for just
      one cent.
    paragraph_summary: The USS John F. Kennedy (CV-67) has embarked on its final journey
      from Philadelphia to Brownsville, Texas, where it will be dismantled after efforts
      to convert it into a museum fell through due to a lack of funding, berthing, and
      long-term maintenance plans. This situation underscores the financial burdens
      associated with retired aircraft carriers, which are often sold for just one cent
      due to the high costs of towing, docking, hazardous-material handling, and regulated
      shipbreaking, despite their significant size and historical importance.
    published: '2026-01-18T17:02:49+00:00'

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/the-trump-class-battleship-has-1-problem-that-no-fancy-pictures-can-fix/
    text: The proposed Trump-class battleship concept depends heavily on a 32-megajoule
      electromagnetic railgun firing hypersonic tungsten projectiles, but railgun feasibility
      remains the central vulnerability. The U.S. Navy’s prior railgun effort ended
      after years of testing and major spending, undermined by cost pressure, combat-system
      integration hurdles, and the extreme electrical power demands railguns impose
      on ships. The post The Trump-Class Battleship Has 1 Problem That No Fancy Pictures
      Can Fix appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The Trump-class battleship concept relies on a 32-megajoule
      electromagnetic railgun, but its feasibility is questionable due to past challenges
      with railgun technology, including high costs, integration issues, and significant
      power requirements.
    paragraph_summary: The Trump-class battleship concept is primarily based on the
      use of a 32-megajoule electromagnetic railgun designed to fire hypersonic tungsten
      projectiles; however, the feasibility of this railgun technology poses a significant
      challenge. The U.S. Navy's previous attempts to develop a railgun were halted
      after extensive testing and substantial investment due to issues such as high
      costs, difficulties in integrating the system with existing combat technologies,
      and the substantial electrical power requirements that railguns demand from ships.

  - title: 'Army Quote of the Day By General George Patton: ‘A Good Plan, Violently
      Executed Now, Is Better Than a Perfect…’'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/army-quote-of-the-by-general-george-patton-a-good-plan-violently-executed-now-is-better-than-a-perfect/
    text: 'U.S. Army General George S. Patton''s earliest battle was personal: dyslexia
      that delayed his ability to read and write until age 11. Family support and relentless
      drive helped him compensate, first at VMI and then at West Point—where academic
      strain forced him to repeat his plebe year after failing math. He ultimately graduated
      and went on to become one of America’s most famous battlefield commanders. The
      post Army Quote of the Day By General George Patton: ‘A Good Plan, Violently Executed
      Now, Is Better Than a Perfect…’ appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: U.S. Army General George S. Patton overcame early struggles
      with dyslexia and academic challenges to become one of America's most renowned
      battlefield commanders.
    paragraph_summary: U.S. Army General George S. Patton faced significant challenges
      early in life due to dyslexia, which hindered his reading and writing skills until
      he was 11. With strong family support and determination, he overcame these obstacles,
      first at the Virginia Military Institute and later at West Point, where he had
      to repeat his plebe year after struggling with math. Despite these setbacks, Patton
      graduated and became one of America's most renowned battlefield commanders, famously
      stating, "A good plan, violently executed now, is better than a perfect plan executed
      later."

  - title: 'Did You Know: The Boeing X-32 Could Have Replaced the F-35 Stealth Fighter'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/did-you-know-the-boeing-x-32-could-have-replaced-the-f-35-stealth-fighter/
    text: 'The Joint Strike Fighter program aimed to cut costs by maximizing commonality
      and using digital modeling to refine requirements before metal was cut. Boeing’s
      X-32 pursued the boldest version of that idea: one basic airframe meant to satisfy
      the Air Force, Navy, and Marines. In practice, that drove compromises—its delta
      wing and large inlet supported carrier needs but constrained performance and raised
      questions about low-speed handling. The post Did You Know: The Boeing X-32 Could
      Have Replaced the F-35 Stealth Fighter appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The Boeing X-32 aimed to streamline the Joint Strike Fighter
      program by using a single airframe for multiple branches of the military, but
      its design compromises raised concerns about performance and handling.
    paragraph_summary: The Joint Strike Fighter program sought to reduce costs through
      increased commonality and digital modeling, with Boeing's X-32 exemplifying this
      approach by designing a single airframe to meet the needs of the Air Force, Navy,
      and Marines. However, this ambition led to compromises, as the X-32's delta wing
      and large inlet, while accommodating carrier operations, negatively impacted performance
      and raised concerns about low-speed handling capabilities.
    published: '2026-01-17T23:38:31+00:00'

  - title: 'Army Quote of the Day by Napoleon: ‘Courage isn’t having the strength to
      go on – it is going on when…’'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/army-quote-of-the-day-by-napoleon-courage-isnt-having-the-strength-to-go-on-it-is-going-on-when/
    text: '“Courage isn’t having the strength to go on…” frames a tour through Napoleon’s
      defining failures and what they reveal about war’s unforgiving variables. Trafalgar
      extinguished French hopes of invading Britain and pushed Napoleon toward economic
      warfare. In Iberia, the Peninsular War turned occupation into attrition, as guerrillas
      bled French forces and morale. The post Army Quote of the Day by Napoleon: ‘Courage
      isn’t having the strength to go on – it is going on when…’ appeared first on 19FortyFive
      .'
    one_sentence_summary: The article explores Napoleon's significant failures, particularly
      at Trafalgar and during the Peninsular War, highlighting how these setbacks shaped
      his military strategies and the harsh realities of warfare.
    paragraph_summary: The article explores Napoleon's significant failures in military
      campaigns, particularly highlighting the Battle of Trafalgar, which dashed French
      ambitions of invading Britain and forced Napoleon to shift to economic warfare.
      It also discusses the challenges faced during the Peninsular War, where guerrilla
      tactics undermined French occupation efforts, leading to attrition in both troops
      and morale. The piece concludes with a reflection on a quote attributed to Napoleon,
      emphasizing that true courage lies in persevering despite adversity.
    published: '2026-01-17T16:09:56+00:00'

  - title: Why the U.S. Navy Quietly Walked Away From Railguns
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/why-the-u-s-navy-quietly-walked-away-from-railguns/
    text: 'U.S. Navy railguns looked like a revolution: electromagnetic launch, hypersonic
      projectiles, long range, and a deep magazine that could ease missile shortages.
      The concept ran into hard constraints—massive power pulses, punishing heat loads,
      accuracy challenges at meaningful ranges, and severe barrel erosion that undercut
      rate of fire and availability. The post Why the U.S. Navy Quietly Walked Away
      From Railguns appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. Navy has abandoned its railgun project due to significant
      technical challenges, including power demands, heat management, accuracy issues,
      and barrel wear that hindered its operational viability.
    paragraph_summary: The U.S. Navy's railgun program, initially seen as a groundbreaking
      advancement in military technology due to its electromagnetic launch capabilities,
      hypersonic projectiles, and potential to alleviate missile shortages, has faced
      significant challenges that led to its decline. Key issues include the need for
      massive power pulses, excessive heat generation, difficulties in maintaining accuracy
      over long distances, and severe barrel erosion that negatively impacted the weapon's
      rate of fire and overall availability. As a result, the Navy has quietly moved
      away from pursuing railgun technology.
    published: '2026-01-17T13:15:17+00:00'

      continuous modernization and iterative software improvements.
    paragraph_summary: The F-35 fighter jet is designed for "continuous modernization,"
      allowing for significant capability enhancements through iterative software updates
      rather than requiring a complete airframe redesign. The upcoming Block 4 upgrade
      aims to improve the aircraft's sensing, targeting, computing power, and weapons
      integration, ensuring its relevance and operational effectiveness for decades
      to come, with projections suggesting it could remain in service until the 2070s.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/navy-supercarrier-uss-gerald-r-ford-is-being-pushed-passed-the-breaking-point/
    text: With no aircraft carrier currently in CENTCOM, the Navy is weighing options
      as tensions rise with Iran—but the Chief of Naval Operations, Adm. Daryl Caudle,
      is pushing back on extending the USS Gerald R. Ford’s already long deployment.
      Ford has been underway since June 24, 2025, and extending beyond the typical timeline
      risks delayed shipyard maintenance, higher costs, and a readiness hit across the
      entire strike group. The post Navy Supercarrier USS Gerald R. Ford Is Being Pushed
      Past the Breaking Point appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: As tensions with Iran escalate and the Navy lacks an aircraft
      carrier in CENTCOM, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle is resisting extending
      the USS Gerald R. Ford's lengthy deployment, which could jeopardize maintenance
      and readiness for the entire strike group.
    paragraph_summary: As tensions with Iran escalate, the Navy is considering its options
      in CENTCOM due to the absence of an aircraft carrier, but Chief of Naval Operations
      Adm. Daryl Caudle is resisting the idea of extending the USS Gerald R. Ford's
      deployment, which has been active since June 24, 2025. Extending this deployment
      could lead to delayed maintenance, increased costs, and negatively impact the
      readiness of the entire strike group.

  - title: The U.S. Navy’s Trump-Class Battleship Might Be a ‘Nuclear Bomber’
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/the-u-s-navys-trump-class-battleship-might-be-a-nuclear-bomber/
    text: 'A proposed Trump-class battleship is framed as a way to refill a naval firepower
      gap—but the bigger question is whether it should carry nuclear capability. The
      argument turns on tradeoffs: adding a mobile surface-launched nuclear option could
      widen presidential choices and complicate an adversary’s targeting calculus, reinforcing
      deterrence if other legs of the force are disrupted. The post The U.S. Navy’s
      Trump-Class Battleship Might Be a ‘Nuclear Bomber’ appeared first on 19FortyFive
      .'
    one_sentence_summary: The proposed Trump-class battleship aims to address naval
      firepower gaps, with a contentious debate over whether it should include nuclear
      capabilities to enhance deterrence and complicate adversary strategies.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the proposal for a Trump-class battleship,
      which aims to address a gap in U.S. naval firepower, while raising the contentious
      issue of whether it should be equipped with nuclear capabilities. Proponents argue
      that incorporating a mobile surface-launched nuclear option could enhance presidential
      decision-making and complicate adversaries' targeting strategies, thereby strengthening
      deterrence, especially if other military assets are compromised. The discussion
      highlights the strategic trade-offs involved in modernizing naval forces.
    published: '2026-01-17T00:20:09+00:00'

  - title: '72,000 Ton Question: The Montana-Class Battleship Is the U.S. Navy’s Big
      ‘What If’'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/72000-ton-question-the-montana-class-battleship-is-the-u-s-navys-big-what-if/
    text: 'The Montana-class battleships sit at the center of a lasting naval “what-if”:
      a larger successor to the Iowa class with heavier armor, a bigger hull, and a
      12-gun 16-inch main battery. They were authorized as the Navy’s final battleship
      order, but the logic of sea power shifted fast. Carrier aviation proved decisive,
      and the Montanas’ slower speed made them ill-suited to operate with fast carrier
      task forces. The post 72,000 Ton Question: The Montana-Class Battleship Is the
      U.S. Navy’s Big ‘What If’ appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The Montana-class battleships represent a significant naval
      "what-if" scenario as a larger, more heavily armed successor to the Iowa class,
      ultimately rendered obsolete by the rise of carrier aviation and the changing
      dynamics of naval warfare.
    paragraph_summary: The Montana-class battleships represent a significant naval "what-if,"
      envisioned as a larger and more powerful successor to the Iowa class, featuring
      heavier armor, a larger hull, and a formidable 12-gun 16-inch main battery. Although
      they were authorized as the final battleship order for the U.S. Navy, the rapid
      evolution of naval warfare, particularly the rise of carrier aviation, rendered
      them impractical due to their slower speed, which hindered their integration with
      fast carrier task forces. The article explores the implications of this shift
      in naval strategy and the Montana-class battleships' place in naval history.
    published: '2026-01-17T00:03:06+00:00'

  - title: 'U.S. Navy Aircraft Carriers: From Supercarrier to Super Target?'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/u-s-navy-aircraft-carriers-from-supercarrier-to-super-target/
    text: 'Aircraft carriers keep getting declared obsolete as submarines, precision
      missiles, drones, cyber, and space targeting raise the cost of operating at sea.
      But obsolescence is the wrong frame. The strategic environment has shifted from
      permissive wars to peer competition, forcing carriers to change how they fight.
      The post U.S. Navy Aircraft Carriers: From Supercarrier to Super Target? appeared
      first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The article argues that while aircraft carriers are often
      deemed obsolete due to advancements in military technology and changing warfare
      dynamics, they must adapt to new strategic challenges rather than being considered
      outdated.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the evolving role of aircraft carriers
      in modern warfare, highlighting that while they have often been deemed obsolete
      due to advancements in submarines, precision missiles, drones, and cyber warfare,
      this perspective is misguided. Instead of viewing carriers as outdated, the article
      argues that the strategic landscape has transitioned from permissive conflicts
      to peer competition, necessitating a transformation in how carriers operate and
      engage in combat. This shift requires carriers to adapt their strategies to remain
      relevant in a more complex and contested maritime environment.
    published: '2026-01-16T23:47:29+00:00'

  - title: The Boeing X-32 Stealth Fighter ‘What If’ Won’t Go Away
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/the-boeing-x-32-stealth-fighter-what-if-wont-go-away/
    text: 'Boeing’s X-32 aimed to win JSF on affordability and manufacturing simplicity,
      anchored by a large one-piece delta wing that boosted internal fuel and reduced
      parts count. Test pilots praised its stable, “F/A-18-like” handling, and the program
      moved fast—two variants, dozens of flights, and a clear focus on practical strike
      performance rather than dogfighting flair. The concept also pointed toward advanced
      sensor integration, with radar work that influenced later Navy systems. The decisive
      issue came in the STOVL phase: Lockheed’s lift-fan approach delivered stronger
      vertical-landing performance, while the X-32’s solution struggled with hot exhaust
      recirculation and overheating. The post The Boeing X-32 Stealth Fighter ‘What
      If’ Won’t Go Away appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Boeing's X-32 fighter aimed to secure the Joint Strike Fighter
      contract through affordability and simplicity, featuring a large delta wing and
      stable handling, but ultimately lost to Lockheed's design due to superior vertical-landing
      performance in the STOVL phase.
    paragraph_summary: Boeing's X-32 was designed to secure the Joint Strike Fighter
      (JSF) contract through its affordability and manufacturing simplicity, featuring
      a large one-piece delta wing that enhanced internal fuel capacity and reduced
      parts count. Test pilots noted its stable handling reminiscent of the F/A-18,
      and the program progressed rapidly with two variants and a focus on practical
      strike capabilities over dogfighting. Additionally, the X-32's advanced sensor
      integration and radar developments influenced future Navy systems. However, the
      critical drawback emerged during the Short Takeoff and Vertical Landing (STOVL)
      phase, where Lockheed's lift-fan design outperformed the X-32, which faced challenges
      with hot exhaust recirculation and overheating.
    published: '2026-01-16T23:36:10+00:00'

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/yf-118g-the-bird-of-prey-stealth-aircraft-no-one-knows-about/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: Boeing’s YF-118G “Bird of Prey”, largely forgotten

      to validate low-cost, rapid design-and-manufacturing methods rather than enter
      operational service. -Developed through McDonnell Douglas’ Phantom Works and later

    one_sentence_summary: Boeing's YF-118G "Bird of Prey" was a stealth technology demonstrator
      designed to validate innovative design and manufacturing methods rather than serve
      in operational roles, featuring advanced radar-evading technologies.
    paragraph_summary: The Boeing YF-118G "Bird of Prey" is a largely overlooked stealth
      technology demonstrator designed as a private venture to test low-cost, rapid
      design and manufacturing methods rather than for operational use. Developed initially
      by McDonnell Douglas' Phantom Works and later by Boeing, the aircraft incorporated
      advanced features such as blended shaping, shielded intakes, and gapless control
      surfaces to minimize radar visibility. Its innovative design aimed to validate
      new approaches in stealth technology, marking a significant, albeit underappreciated,
      contribution to aerospace development.

    paragraph_summary: 'China''s anti-access/area denial (A2/AD) strategy is centered
      around three key components: drones, missiles, and submarines, designed to deter
      U.S. carrier strike groups from operating within the first island chain. This
      strategy includes advanced weaponry such as carrier-killer ballistic missiles
      like the DF-21D and DF-26, sea-skimming YJ-series missiles launched from Type
      055 destroyers and H-6K bombers, as well as stealthier Type 093B and 096 submarines.
      Collectively, these elements create a formidable defense aimed at making the region
      a no-go zone for U.S. naval forces.'

      concept could offer valuable insights for the U.S. Air Force in modern aerial
      combat strategies.

      rapid movement, and taking the initiative to prevent the enemy from regrouping.
      He effectively combined maneuver warfare, utilizing tanks and motorized infantry
      alongside coordinated arms, while maintaining a strong focus on logistics to ensure
      that fast advances were supported by adequate fuel and ammunition. His successful
      campaigns, particularly after restoring discipline following the Kasserine Pass,
      exemplified this approach, underscoring his belief that successful defense is

    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. Navy's railgun concept has failed due to practical
      challenges such as power demands, heat management, and accuracy issues, highlighting
      the need for realistic alternatives like hypersonic missiles.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the challenges faced by the U.S. Navy in
      implementing railgun technology, which was initially promising due to its potential
      for hypersonic projectiles, extensive ammunition capacity, and low cost per shot.
      However, the concept has failed to materialize effectively due to practical issues
      such as the immense power requirements, heat generation, cooling limitations,
      accuracy problems, and significant barrel wear. Furthermore, the integration of
      railguns into existing Burke-class ships was problematic, as they were not designed
      to handle the energy demands, and even the Zumwalt-class ships had limited power
      capacity. Ultimately, the article concludes that while railguns remain unfeasible,
      the development of hypersonic missiles capable of reaching Mach 6 is a tangible
      reality.

      quiet operation, and ease of use, with advancements seen in various project iterations
      and notable sales to countries like China and Iran.
    paragraph_summary: The Kilo-class submarines, originally developed during the Cold
      War, have become popular export models for Russia due to their compact design,
      quiet operation, and simple diesel-electric systems. The class includes various
      iterations, with Project 877 serving as the baseline, Project 636 enhancing automation
      and stealth capabilities, and Project 636.3 continuing the evolution of the design
      amid delays with the Lada-class submarines. These submarines have been sold to
      countries like China and Iran, earning the nickname "Black Hole" for their stealth
      features.

      of body composition among troops.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/breakthrough-navy-nuclear-submarines-now-get-protection-from-weld-cracks-with-neutron-beam/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: Researchers from the U.S. Navy, Electric Boat, and
      the University of Connecticut have developed a breakthrough method using “neutron
      beams” to inspect submarine hulls for microscopic flaws. -Unlike X-rays, neutron
      beams can deeply penetrate thick steel without damaging it, allowing engineers
      to detect internal stress, “ductility dip cracking,” and weld defects […] The
      post Breakthrough: Navy Nuclear Submarines Now Get Protection From Weld Cracks
      with Neutron Beam appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Researchers have developed a new method using neutron beams
      to inspect submarine hulls for microscopic flaws, enabling the detection of internal
      stress and weld defects without damaging the thick steel.
    paragraph_summary: Researchers from the U.S. Navy, Electric Boat, and the University
      of Connecticut have introduced an innovative technique utilizing neutron beams
      to inspect submarine hulls for microscopic flaws. This method offers significant
      advantages over traditional X-ray inspections, as neutron beams can penetrate
      thick steel without causing damage, enabling the detection of internal stresses,
      ductility dip cracking, and weld defects. This breakthrough enhances the safety
      and reliability of Navy nuclear submarines by providing better protection against
      potential structural issues.

  - title: Mandatory 2-Mile Run In Fitness Test Eliminated by the Air Force
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/mandatory-2-mile-run-in-fitness-test-eliminated-by-the-air-force/
    text: 'Synopsis: The U.S. Air Force has rescinded its mandate requiring airmen to
      complete a two-mile run annually, instead allowing them to choose between the
      run and the 20-meter High Aerobic Multi-shuttle Run (HAMR) for their bi-annual
      fitness tests. -While the Space Force will maintain the mandatory run for Guardians,
      the Air Force’s new policy begins […] The post Mandatory 2-Mile Run In Fitness
      Test Eliminated by the Air Force appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. Air Force has eliminated the mandatory annual two-mile
      run for airmen, allowing them to choose between the run and the 20-meter High
      Aerobic Multi-shuttle Run (HAMR) for their bi-annual fitness tests, while the
      Space Force will continue to require the run for Guardians.
    paragraph_summary: The U.S. Air Force has eliminated its requirement for airmen
      to complete an annual two-mile run as part of their fitness tests, now allowing
      them to choose between the run and the 20-meter High Aerobic Multi-shuttle Run
      (HAMR) for their bi-annual assessments. In contrast, the Space Force will continue
      to require the two-mile run for its Guardians. This policy change reflects a shift
      in the Air Force's approach to physical fitness testing.
    published: '2026-01-13T12:29:01+00:00'

      technology for its time.

      and populations committed to national self-determination. This shift in dynamics
      makes the imposition of spheres of influence increasingly untenable.

      soldier to address suicide prevention during the 2025 holiday season.
    paragraph_summary: The U.S. Army has initiated the "Just Pick Up" campaign, spearheaded
      by Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, to address the critical issue of suicide among
      soldiers during the 2025 holiday season. This initiative mandates that officers
      and non-commissioned officers (NCOs) personally check in with every soldier daily
      until January 15, 2026. The campaign draws inspiration from a successful strategy
      implemented by the 11th Airborne Division, aiming to foster connection and support
      within the ranks to prevent suicide and promote mental well-being.

    text: 'Synopsis: William Tecumseh Sherman, famous for declaring “War is hell,” remains
      one of the Civil War’s most complex figures. -Overcoming early career struggles

      S. Grant that led to Union victories at Vicksburg and Shiloh. -He is best remembered

    one_sentence_summary: William Tecumseh Sherman, a complex Civil War figure known
      for his partnership with Ulysses S. Grant and his infamous "March to the Sea,"
      expressed deep disillusionment with war, famously stating, "I am tired and sick
      of war. Its glory is all moonshine."
    paragraph_summary: William Tecumseh Sherman, known for his famous quote "War is
      hell," is a complex figure in Civil War history who overcame early career challenges
      and accusations of insanity to become a key military leader. His partnership with
      Ulysses S. Grant was instrumental in securing Union victories at significant battles
      such as Vicksburg and Shiloh. Sherman is particularly remembered for his 1864
      "March to the Sea," which exemplified his belief that war's glory is illusory
      and that its true nature is destructive and exhausting.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/military-quote-of-the-day-by-socrates-all-wars-are-fought-for-money/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – Best known as the father of Western philosophy,
      Socrates was also a disciplined soldier who served as a hoplite in the Peloponnesian
      War, fighting in the battles of Potidaea, Delium, and Amphipolis. -Despite his
      bravery on the battlefield—where he once saved the life of Alcibiades—Socrates
      famously argued in Plato’s Phaedo […] The post Military Quote of the Day by Socrates:
      ‘All Wars are Fought for Money…’ appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Socrates, renowned as the father of Western philosophy and
      a courageous hoplite in the Peloponnesian War, controversially stated in Plato's
      Phaedo that all wars are fought for money, despite his own acts of bravery on
      the battlefield.
    paragraph_summary: Socrates, renowned as the father of Western philosophy, was also
      a dedicated soldier who fought as a hoplite in the Peloponnesian War, participating
      in key battles such as Potidaea, Delium, and Amphipolis, where he notably saved
      Alcibiades' life. Despite his military valor, Socrates expressed a critical view
      of war, famously stating in Plato's "Phaedo" that "All wars are fought for money,"
      highlighting his belief in the underlying economic motivations behind conflict.
    published: '2026-01-12T15:19:35+00:00'

    one_sentence_summary: The article examines the quote "He that waits upon fortune

      despite uncertainty about its true authorship.
    paragraph_summary: The article examines the quote “He that waits upon fortune is
      never sure of a dinner,” often linked to Benjamin Franklin, although it suggests
      he may not have originated it. The saying reflects the themes of industriousness
      and frugality found in Franklin's "Poor Richard’s Almanack," published between
      1732 and 1758. The piece emphasizes the importance of taking initiative rather
      than relying on luck, aligning with Franklin's broader philosophy on self-reliance
      and hard work.

    text: 'Key Points and Summary – In the 1970s and 80s, the U.S. Navy considered converting
      Iowa-class battleships into “battlecarriers” equipped with flight decks for STOVL
      aircraft and massive firepower, including 320-tube vertical launch systems. -Proposed
      by military reformer Charles E. Myers to provide littoral fire support, the radical
      “Phase II” plan was ultimately scrapped due […] The post Forget the Trump-Class
      Battleship: The Navy’s Iowa-Class Nearly Became an ‘Aircraft Carrier’ appeared
      first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: In the 1970s and 80s, the U.S. Navy explored converting Iowa-class
      battleships into "battlecarriers" with flight decks and advanced weaponry for
      littoral support, but the ambitious plan was ultimately abandoned.
    paragraph_summary: In the 1970s and 80s, the U.S. Navy explored the idea of transforming
      Iowa-class battleships into "battlecarriers" designed to support short takeoff
      and vertical landing (STOVL) aircraft and equipped with significant firepower,
      including 320-tube vertical launch systems. This innovative concept, proposed
      by military reformer Charles E. Myers, aimed to enhance littoral fire support
      capabilities. However, the ambitious "Phase II" plan was ultimately abandoned,
      marking a notable moment in naval history as the Navy reconsidered its approach
      to battleship design and functionality.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/the-experimental-f-16xl-fighter-was-dumped-by-the-air-force-and-sent-to-nasa/
    text: Key Points and Summary – The F-16XL was a revolutionary “cranked-arrow” delta
      wing variant of the F-16 designed for long-range, high-speed strike missions.
      -Despite superior aerodynamics, fuel efficiency, and a massive 27-hardpoint payload,
      it lost the USAF’s Enhanced Tactical Fighter competition to the F-15E Strike Eagle.

    one_sentence_summary: The F-16XL, an advanced variant of the F-16 with superior
      aerodynamics and payload capacity, was ultimately rejected by the Air Force in
      favor of the F-15E Strike Eagle due to its twin-engine design, and was subsequently
      transferred to NASA.
    paragraph_summary: The F-16XL was an innovative variant of the F-16 featuring a
      "cranked-arrow" delta wing design, aimed at enhancing long-range, high-speed strike
      capabilities with superior aerodynamics, fuel efficiency, and a substantial 27-hardpoint
      payload. Despite these advantages, it lost the USAF's Enhanced Tactical Fighter
      competition to the F-15E Strike Eagle, which was preferred for its twin-engine
      redundancy. Following its defeat, the F-16XL was ultimately retired from military
      consideration and transferred to NASA for further research and development.

    text: 'Synopsis: Despite the invention of autopilot in 1912 by Lawrence Sperry,
      U.S. Naval Aviators generally refuse to use it for landing on aircraft carriers.
      -According to former EA-18G Growler pilot Adam Daymude, while autopilot works
      in calm conditions, it struggles unpredictably in rough weather, with auto-throttle
      systems occasionally cutting power at critical moments. -Consequently, pilots
      […] The post Why U.S. Navy Pilots Refuse to Use ‘Autopilot’ for Aircraft Carrier
      Landings appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: U.S. Navy pilots avoid using autopilot for aircraft carrier
      landings due to its unreliable performance in rough weather and the risk of auto-throttle
      systems cutting power at critical moments.
    paragraph_summary: Despite the development of autopilot technology by Lawrence Sperry
      in 1912, U.S. Naval Aviators are hesitant to use it for landing on aircraft carriers.
      Former EA-18G Growler pilot Adam Daymude explains that while autopilot functions
      well in stable conditions, it can be unreliable in turbulent weather, with auto-throttle
      systems sometimes reducing power at crucial moments. As a result, pilots prefer
      to manually land their aircraft to ensure safety and control during these challenging
      operations.

    text: Key Points and Summary – As China’s anti-ship capabilities grow, questions

      their bulk, high power requirements, and design optimization for fixed land sites.

    one_sentence_summary: Experts contend that equipping U.S. Navy vessels with land-based
      missile defense systems like THAAD or PAC-3 is impractical due to their size and
      design limitations, suggesting that the Navy should instead focus on alternative
      defense strategies against China's growing anti-ship capabilities.
    paragraph_summary: As China's anti-ship capabilities expand, there is debate over
      the feasibility of equipping U.S. Navy vessels with land-based missile defense
      systems like THAAD or PAC-3. Experts contend that these systems are not suitable
      for maritime environments due to their size, high power demands, and design focus
      on stationary land installations. Consequently, the Navy is expected to continue
      relying on its existing naval defense strategies rather than adopting these land-based
      systems for ship protection against potential Chinese missile threats.

    text: 'Key Points and Synopsis: In a rare personnel move, U.S. Army Master Sergeant

    one_sentence_summary: U.S. Army Master Sergeant Jeremy Chambers has made history
      by being directly promoted to Captain, bypassing the lieutenant ranks, to serve
      as a Foreign Area Officer, a move supported by Lt. Gen. Jonathan Braga to utilize
      his extensive enlisted expertise.
    paragraph_summary: U.S. Army Master Sergeant Jeremy Chambers has made history by
      being promoted directly to the rank of Captain (O-3), bypassing the usual lieutenant
      ranks, in a rare personnel decision supported by Lt. Gen. Jonathan Braga. This
      promotion aims to utilize Chambers' extensive enlisted experience in his new role
      as a Foreign Area Officer (FAO), which necessitates proficiency in foreign languages
      and cultural understanding. Chambers is the first non-commissioned officer (NCO)
      in the U.S. Army to achieve this direct commission as a FAO captain.

      interventions in their regions. This situation is particularly concerning for
      Russia, as it may validate its imperialist ambitions and heighten the risk of
      invasions in neighboring countries such as Moldova, Georgia, and the Baltic states.
      The piece suggests that the crisis in Venezuela could have far-reaching consequences
      for Russia's geopolitical stance and stability in its vicinity.

      and military endeavors.

      amidst ongoing trade tensions.

      by strategically positioning his troops behind a ridge, ultimately leading to

      in battle.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/the-new-b-21-raider-stealth-bomber-has-a-message-for-the-u-s-air-force/
    text: 'Sunopsis: The U.S. Air Force currently plans to buy 100 B-21 Raider stealth
      bombers, but experts like Dr. Rebecca Grant and the Center for Strategic and Budgetary
      Assessments argue this number is dangerously low. -Citing China’s December 2024

      recommend doubling the fleet […] The post The New B-21 Raider Stealth Bomber Has

    one_sentence_summary: Experts warn that the U.S. Air Force's plan to acquire 100
      B-21 Raider stealth bombers is insufficient in light of emerging threats from
      China's new stealth aircraft, suggesting that the fleet size should be doubled.
    paragraph_summary: The U.S. Air Force intends to acquire 100 B-21 Raider stealth
      bombers, but experts, including Dr. Rebecca Grant and the Center for Strategic
      and Budgetary Assessments, believe this figure is insufficient given emerging
      threats, particularly from China, which is set to unveil two new stealth aircraft
      by December 2024 aimed at challenging U.S. positions in Guam and Hawaii. Analysts
      are advocating for the Air Force to double its planned fleet to better address
      these potential security challenges.

    one_sentence_summary: The article draws parallels between Napoleon Bonaparte's 1815
      return from exile and current political challenges in Western democracies, highlighting
      that recovering from defeat, as seen with leaders like Emmanuel Macron and Donald
      Trump, does not ensure enduring success or authority.
    paragraph_summary: The article draws a parallel between Napoleon Bonaparte's 1815
      return from exile and the current political landscape in Western democracies,
      highlighting that recovering from defeat does not ensure enduring success. It
      notes that in France, President Emmanuel Macron faces political paralysis despite
      remaining in office after the 2024 snap elections, while in the U.S., Donald Trump
      is attempting to regain influence. The piece underscores the idea that, like Napoleon,
      contemporary leaders must navigate the complexities of political recovery and
      authority in the face of setbacks.

    text: Key Points and Summary – In a “quiet” but high-stakes 1997 operation, the
      U.S. purchased 21 Soviet-made MiG-29 fighters from Moldova to prevent them from
      falling into Iranian hands. -Fearing Iran would use the “nuclear-capable” aircraft
      to deliver WMDs, Washington paid $40 million under the Nunn-Lugar program to secure
      the fleet. -The jets were flown […] The post The U.S. Military Purchased 21 Russian-Made

    one_sentence_summary: In a covert 1997 operation, the U.S. purchased 21 Soviet-made
      MiG-29 fighters from Moldova for $40 million to prevent them from being acquired
      by Iran, which could have used the aircraft to deliver weapons of mass destruction.
    paragraph_summary: In a discreet yet critical operation in 1997, the U.S. acquired
      21 Soviet-made MiG-29 fighters from Moldova for $40 million under the Nunn-Lugar
      program, aiming to prevent these aircraft from potentially falling into Iranian
      hands. The U.S. government was concerned that Iran could utilize these "nuclear-capable"
      jets to deliver weapons of mass destruction. The operation highlighted the strategic
      importance of securing military assets in post-Soviet states to mitigate risks
      associated with proliferation.

    text: 'Synopsis: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) reached a $2.5 billion settlement
      with Amazon over allegations of “deceptive” tactics used to trap consumers in
      Prime subscriptions. -While $1 billion serves as a civil penalty, $1.5 billion
      is allocated for consumer refunds, capped at $51 per person. -Automatic refunds

    one_sentence_summary: The FTC has settled with Amazon for $2.5 billion over deceptive
      Prime subscription practices, with $1 billion as a civil penalty and $1.5 billion
      for consumer refunds, allowing eligible customers to file claims for up to $51
      each.
    paragraph_summary: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has settled with Amazon for
      $2.5 billion due to claims of deceptive practices that entangled consumers in
      Prime subscriptions. Of this amount, $1 billion is designated as a civil penalty,
      while $1.5 billion is set aside for consumer refunds, with individual refunds
      capped at $51. Automatic refunds were issued in late 2025, and eligible customers
      can also file claims to receive their payments under the settlement.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/40-months-why-u-s-navy-nuclear-submarines-take-so-long-to-refuel/
    text: Key Points and Summary – Nuclear-powered submarines offer extraordinary endurance,
      but when refueling finally arrives, it is a painstaking industrial event—not a
      simple “fill-up.” -The boat must be placed in dry dock, powered down under strict
      radiation controls, and opened up so specialists can access a reactor buried behind
      heavy shielding. -Crews remove and log […] The post 40 Months? Why U.S. Navy Nuclear
      Submarines Take So Long to ‘Refuel’ appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: Refueling U.S. Navy nuclear submarines is a complex and lengthy
      process that requires dry docking, strict radiation controls, and specialized
      access to the reactor, making it far more involved than a simple fuel refill.
    paragraph_summary: Nuclear-powered submarines provide remarkable endurance, but
      their refueling process is complex and time-consuming, requiring the submarine
      to be placed in dry dock and powered down under strict radiation controls. Specialists
      must access the reactor, which is heavily shielded, leading to a meticulous procedure
      where crews remove and log components for replacement. This intricate industrial
      event can take up to 40 months, highlighting the challenges associated with maintaining
      these advanced vessels.

    text: 'Key Points and Summary – The “F-35 Ferrari” idea argues Lockheed could funnel

      Block 4 improvements. -The pitch centers on more power, better sensors and computing,
      stronger electronic warfare, manned-unmanned teaming, and—most controversially—an

    one_sentence_summary: The "F-35 Ferrari" concept suggests that Lockheed Martin could
      significantly enhance the F-35 by integrating advanced technologies from the Next
      Generation Air Dominance (NGAD) program, but experts remain skeptical about the
      feasibility of such a transformation.
    paragraph_summary: The "F-35 Ferrari" concept suggests that Lockheed Martin could
      integrate advanced technologies from the Next Generation Air Dominance (NGAD)
      program into the F-35, aiming for significant enhancements rather than just incremental
      updates with Block 4 improvements. This proposal emphasizes upgrades in power,
      sensors, computing capabilities, electronic warfare, and manned-unmanned teaming,
      with the most contentious aspect being the introduction of an adaptive-cycle engine
      to improve range and thermal performance. However, the article ultimately argues
      that the F-35 will not evolve into the envisioned F-47 NGAD fighter.

  - title: 'Autopilot Works Until It Doesn’t: The Aircraft Carrier Landing Lesson From
      a U.S. Navy EA-18G Growler Pilot'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/autopilot-works-until-it-doesnt-the-aircraft-carrier-landing-lesson-from-a-u-s-navy-ea-18g-growler-pilot/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – Autopilot can be impressive in cruise flight. Still,
      aircraft carrier landings are a different problem: a pitching deck, variable winds,
      and razor-thin margins that punish even minor errors. -Using a former EA-18G Growler
      pilot’s account, this article explains why Naval Aviators distrust full auto-recoveries—and
      why auto-throttle can be flawless for […] The post Autopilot Works Until It Doesn’t:
      The Aircraft Carrier Landing Lesson From a U.S. Navy EA-18G Growler Pilot appeared
      first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The article highlights the limitations of autopilot systems
      in the challenging environment of aircraft carrier landings, emphasizing a former
      EA-18G Growler pilot's perspective on the distrust of full auto-recoveries due
      to the complexities of a pitching deck and variable conditions.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the limitations of autopilot systems in
      the context of aircraft carrier landings, highlighting the challenges posed by
      a moving deck, changing winds, and the need for precision. Using insights from
      a former EA-18G Growler pilot, it emphasizes the skepticism among Naval Aviators
      regarding full auto-recoveries, despite the reliability of auto-throttle systems
      during cruise flight. The piece illustrates that while autopilot can perform well
      in stable conditions, the complexities of carrier landings require a level of
      human judgment and control that automation cannot fully provide.
    published: '2026-01-05T15:06:23+00:00'

    text: 'Synopsis: Napoleon understood that winning often means controlling chaos—but

      of control.
    paragraph_summary: 'The article examines Napoleon''s military career, highlighting
      how his operational genius often clashed with strategic limitations, leading to
      significant setbacks in three key campaigns: the Egyptian campaign, which was
      thwarted by Nelson''s decisive victory at the Battle of the Nile; the Russian
      campaign, where tactics like scorched earth and the fierce Battle of Borodino
      turned his occupation into a disastrous retreat; and other instances where his
      attempts to control chaos on the battlefield ultimately slipped away, underscoring
      the precarious nature of military success.'

      security forces, potentially leading to civil conflict by 2026.

      the potential threat they pose.

  - title: 'Forget the Trump-Class Battleship: The Navy’s Iowa-Class Was Almost an ‘Aircraft
      Carrier’'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/forget-the-trump-class-battleship-the-navys-iowa-class-was-almost-an-aircraft-carrier/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – In the late 1970s and early 1980s, Navy thinkers
      repeatedly revisited a radical idea: convert Iowa-class battleships into ‘battlecarriers’
      or interdiction/assault ships, adding a flight deck for STOVL aircraft and, in
      later concepts, an enormous missile battery—up to a 320-tube VLS—alongside big
      guns and space for Marines and SEALs. -Advocates […] The post Forget the Trump-Class
      Battleship: The Navy’s Iowa-Class Was Almost an ‘Aircraft Carrier’ appeared first
      on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: In the late 1970s and early 1980s, Navy strategists considered
      transforming Iowa-class battleships into hybrid 'battlecarriers' equipped with
      flight decks for STOVL aircraft, extensive missile systems, and space for Marines
      and SEALs.
    paragraph_summary: In the late 1970s and early 1980s, U.S. Navy strategists explored
      the innovative concept of transforming Iowa-class battleships into 'battlecarriers'
      or interdiction/assault ships. This transformation would involve adding a flight
      deck for Short Takeoff and Vertical Landing (STOVL) aircraft, as well as incorporating
      a substantial missile battery—potentially featuring up to 320 Vertical Launch

  - title: Donald Trump’s Venezuela Strike Summed Up in 2 Words
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/donald-trumps-venezuela-strike-summed-up-in-2-words/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – The early takes on Venezuela—imperialism, political
      diversion, oil grab—miss the central logic: hemispheric denial. -In 2 Words: Framed
      as the “Donroe Doctrine,” the argument is that Washington will block hostile great-power
      entrenchment in the Western Hemisphere, and Venezuela had become the most advanced
      test case for Russian, Chinese, and Iranian […] The post Donald Trump’s Venezuela
      Strike Summed Up in 2 Words appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The article argues that the U.S. response to Venezuela is
      primarily driven by a desire to prevent hostile foreign influence in the region,
      framed as a modern iteration of the Monroe Doctrine.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the U.S. perspective on Venezuela, framing
      it as a critical case in the context of the "Donroe Doctrine," which suggests
      that Washington aims to prevent the influence of hostile great powers like Russia,
      China, and Iran in the Western Hemisphere. It argues that early interpretations
      of the situation—viewing it through the lenses of imperialism, political diversion,
      or oil interests—miss the fundamental issue of hemispheric denial, emphasizing
      that Venezuela has become a significant battleground for geopolitical influence.

      dubbed the "fifth-generation-plus" or "Ferrari" variant, which incorporates select
      technologies from its Next Generation Air Dominance (NGAD) program. The key selling
      points of this enhanced F-35 are its potential for rapid deployment and the ability
      to produce it in larger quantities compared to developing a completely new sixth-generation
      fighter jet. This strategy aims to provide the U.S. Air Force with a more immediate
      and scalable solution for modern aerial combat.

      B-52 bombers. This initiative signals a commitment to modernizing the B-52J Stratofortress,
      ensuring its continued relevance and operational capability in the Air Force's
      strategic arsenal.

    text: 'Synopsis: This piece argues that a U.S. raid capturing Nicolás Maduro—paired

      to crush a democratic, sovereign choice and to reassert imperial claims. -At the
      same time, the U.S. objective in Venezuela […] The post Venezuela Isn’t Ukraine

    one_sentence_summary: The article contends that while a U.S. raid to capture Nicolás
      Maduro might mirror Russia's failed decapitation attempt in Ukraine in execution,
      the underlying motivations differ significantly, as the U.S. aims to support democracy
      in Venezuela rather than assert imperial ambitions.
    paragraph_summary: The article contends that a U.S. operation to capture Nicolás
      Maduro, alongside a wider military campaign, might mimic Russia's unsuccessful
      attempt to decapitate Ukraine's leadership, but the underlying motivations differ
      significantly. While Putin's invasion aimed to undermine Ukraine's democratic
      sovereignty and reinforce imperial ambitions, the U.S. objectives in Venezuela
      are framed within a different context, suggesting a focus on restoring democracy
      rather than imperialism. The author emphasizes that despite superficial similarities
      in tactics, the geopolitical implications and intentions behind U.S. actions in
      Venezuela are distinct from Russia's actions in Ukraine.

    text: 'Key Points and Summary – The proposed Trump-class battleship shocked observers

      packed with vertical-launch cells, hypersonic strike capacity, and layered defenses

    one_sentence_summary: The proposed Trump-class battleship, which contrasts with
      the Navy's trend towards smaller forces, is envisioned as a heavily armed surface
      combatant designed to serve as a "floating arsenal" with advanced missile capabilities
      and defenses.

      its contradiction with the Navy's trend towards smaller, more distributed forces.
      However, proponents argue that this large surface combatant, designed as a "floating
      arsenal," could effectively serve military purposes by incorporating numerous
      vertical-launch cells, hypersonic strike capabilities, and advanced layered defenses.
      This design aims to secure vital sea lanes and deny access to adversaries, positioning

    one_sentence_summary: The article discusses a quote often attributed to Benjamin

    paragraph_summary: The article discusses a quote often attributed to Benjamin Franklin
      that contrasts war and revolution, highlighting that in war, the government identifies
      the enemy, while in revolution, the people determine their oppressors. This distinction
      reflects the mindset of colonists in 1775, a time when many were beginning to
      question British authority and consider the nature of their struggle for independence.
      The piece emphasizes the psychological shift from viewing conflict as a government-defined
      war to recognizing it as a revolutionary movement driven by the people's agency.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/u-s-navy-quote-of-the-day-by-theodore-roosevelt-a-good-navy-is-not-a-provocation-to-war-it-is-the-surest-guarantee-of-peace/
    text: 'Synopsis: Theodore Roosevelt’s 1902 warning—“A good Navy is not a provocation
      to war. It is the surest guarantee of peace”—captures the logic behind his “Big
      Stick” worldview: credible power deters conflict, protects trade, and gives diplomacy
      leverage. -From his rise as assistant secretary of the Navy to the Rough Riders
      and ultimately the presidency, Roosevelt […] The post U.S. Navy Quote of the Day
      by Theodore Roosevelt: ‘A good Navy is not a provocation to war. It is the surest
      guarantee of peace’ appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The article highlights Theodore Roosevelt's belief that a
      strong Navy serves as a deterrent to war and a means to ensure peace, reflecting
      his "Big Stick" approach to foreign policy.
    paragraph_summary: The article highlights Theodore Roosevelt's belief in the importance
      of a strong Navy as a means to ensure peace, encapsulated in his 1902 quote, “A
      good Navy is not a provocation to war. It is the surest guarantee of peace.” This
      perspective reflects his "Big Stick" philosophy, which emphasizes that credible
      military power can deter conflict, safeguard trade, and enhance diplomatic efforts.
      The piece traces Roosevelt's journey from assistant secretary of the Navy to his
      presidency, illustrating how his experiences shaped his views on naval strength
      and its role in international relations.

      and cohesion in military operations.

      "A pint of sweat will save a gallon of blood," highlighting its significance as
      both a motivational mantra and an operational strategy. Patton emphasized the

      cohesion, and speed among troops, ultimately aiming to minimize preventable casualties
      on the battlefield. This philosophy was evident in his approach at the Desert
      Training Center and during the Third Army's preparations for invasion, reflecting
      his belief that thorough preparation could save lives in combat.

  - title: 'Military Quote of the Day by Plato: ‘Only The Dead Have Seen The End Of
      War’'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/military-quote-of-the-day-by-plato-only-the-dead-have-seen-the-end-of-war/
    text: 'Synopsis: “Only the dead have seen the end of war” is widely shared as a
      Plato quote, but the piece argues its real roots trace to George Santayana’s post–World
      War I writing, rejecting the comforting idea that any conflict will truly end
      all others. -The misattribution spread further when Gen. Douglas MacArthur quoted
      the line […] The post Military Quote of the Day by Plato: ‘Only The Dead Have
      Seen The End Of War’ appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The article clarifies that the quote "Only the dead have seen
      the end of war," often misattributed to Plato, actually originates from George
      Santayana's post-World War I writings, emphasizing the idea that conflicts are
      unlikely to ever truly cease.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the misattribution of the quote "Only the
      dead have seen the end of war," often credited to Plato, but actually originating
      from George Santayana's writings after World War I. It highlights how this quote
      challenges the notion that any single conflict can definitively end all wars.
      The misattribution gained further traction when General Douglas MacArthur cited
      the line, reinforcing its prevalence in military discourse despite its true origins.
    published: '2026-01-02T16:27:48+00:00'

    text: 'Synopsis: A quote often linked to Benjamin Franklin draws a blunt distinction:

    one_sentence_summary: The article discusses a quote attributed to Benjamin Franklin

      of pre-1776 American colonists.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses a quote attributed to Benjamin Franklin

      designated enemies, while revolution arises when individuals identify their own
      oppressors. This perspective aligns with the mindset of pre-1776 American colonists,
      who viewed themselves as English subjects fighting against unfair representation
      rather than outright rejecting the British crown. The piece reflects on the implications
      of this distinction in understanding the nature of conflict and resistance.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/01/forget-the-trump-class-battleship-the-u-s-navys-iowa-class-almost-became-an-aircraft-carrier/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – This article argues that today’s “Trump-class battleship”
      idea has historical echoes in the Navy’s recurring fascination with oversized,
      heavily armed surface ships. -During WWII, U.S. planners explored converting Iowa-class
      hulls into carrier-like vessels as carrier shortages loomed in the Pacific. -Decades
      later, a late-1970s concept revived the idea: an Iowa […] The post Forget the
      Trump-Class Battleship: The U.S. Navy’s Iowa-Class Almost Became an ‘Aircraft
      Carrier’ appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The article discusses the historical parallels between the
      current "Trump-class battleship" concept and past U.S. Navy efforts, particularly
      during WWII and the late 1970s, to repurpose Iowa-class battleships into aircraft
      carriers amid naval challenges.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the historical parallels between the current
      "Trump-class battleship" concept and the U.S. Navy's past interest in large, heavily
      armed surface ships, particularly the Iowa-class battleships. During World War
      II, U.S. military planners considered modifying Iowa-class hulls into aircraft
      carriers due to a shortage of carriers in the Pacific. This idea resurfaced in
      the late 1970s, highlighting a recurring theme in naval strategy of adapting existing
      battleship designs for new roles. The piece ultimately critiques the contemporary
      fascination with oversized battleships by reflecting on these historical attempts
      to repurpose Iowa-class vessels.

    one_sentence_summary: Pete Hegseth suggests that while reorganizing combatant commands
      is a consideration, the more significant challenge lies in reforming the military
      services themselves, which continue to hinder adaptation due to their dominance
      in procurement, training, and doctrine.
    paragraph_summary: Pete Hegseth has proposed the idea of reorganizing U.S. combatant
      commands, but he emphasizes that a more significant challenge lies in reforming

      military's ability to adapt swiftly to the rapidly changing nature of modern warfare.
      The establishment of the Air Force and Space Force demonstrates that the U.S.
      is capable of institutional reform, suggesting that similar changes could be beneficial
      for the overall effectiveness of the military.

      is accelerating the development of the XM30 infantry fighting vehicle to enhance
      its tactical effectiveness and protection in a rapidly evolving battlefield environment.

    one_sentence_summary: The proposed Trump-class battleship (BBG(X)) raises concerns
      similar to Russia's Kirov-class, as its extensive missile capabilities may lead
      to costly upgrades and challenges in fleet integration, highlighting the potential
      pitfalls of mega-surface combatants.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the proposed Trump-class "battleship" (BBG(X)),
      which aims to feature a large missile magazine on a single hull, drawing parallels
      to Russia's Kirov-class warships. It highlights the challenges faced by Admiral
      Nakhimov, whose lengthy modernization process exemplifies the pitfalls of mega-surface
      combatants, which can become costly to upgrade, difficult to protect, and slow
      to deploy back into service. Despite advancements in long-range missiles and enhanced
      defenses, the article suggests that such large vessels may ultimately be more
      of a financial burden than a strategic asset for naval forces.

    text: Key Points and Summary – Europe’s flagship next-generation fighter effort,
      FCAS, just missed another decision deadline—with no verdict from Berlin or Paris
      and no new timeline in sight. -The program, launched in 2017 to replace Rafale
      and Eurofighter fleets around 2040, has stalled as France’s Dassault and Airbus
      (backing German and Spanish interests) clash over […] The post F-35 and F-47 Win?

    one_sentence_summary: Europe's FCAS next-generation fighter program has stalled
      due to conflicts between France's Dassault and Airbus, missing another decision
      deadline with no new timeline, raising concerns that it may never be realized.
    paragraph_summary: The Future Combat Air System (FCAS), Europe's ambitious next-generation
      fighter program aimed at replacing the Rafale and Eurofighter fleets by 2040,
      has encountered significant delays, missing another decision deadline without
      any resolution from Berlin or Paris and lacking a new timeline. Launched in 2017,
      the initiative has stalled due to ongoing conflicts between France's Dassault
      and Airbus, which represents German and Spanish interests, raising concerns that
      the FCAS may never materialize, potentially benefiting competitors like the F-35
      and F-47.

    text: 'Synopsis: China is moving from a domestic fighter producer to a global exporter

      the stealth-capable FC-31/J-35, the versatile J-10C, and the budget-friendly JF-17,
      appealing to international buyers with fewer political restrictions.

      to a global exporter, offering a diverse three-tier portfolio of aircraft. This

      multirole fighter equipped with modern sensors and long-range missiles, and the
      budget-friendly JF-17 designed for affordability and ease of logistics. The appeal
      of these Chinese fighter jets lies in their reduced political restrictions compared
      to Western options like the F-16 and F-35, making them attractive to potential
      buyers.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/the-air-forces-new-playbook-f-47-penetrator-f-22-enforcer-f-35-quarterback/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – The Air Force is heading toward a three-tier air-dominance
      model instead of betting everything on one jet. -The F-47 NGAD is positioned as
      the deep-penetrating quarterback for contested fights, built to plug into a broader
      family of systems, including loyal-wingman drones. -At the same time, a viability
      upgrade package could […] The post The Air Force’s New Playbook: F-47 Penetrator,
      F-22 Enforcer, F-35 Quarterback appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The Air Force is adopting a three-tier air-dominance strategy
      featuring the F-47 NGAD as a deep-penetrating leader, supported by loyal-wingman
      drones, alongside upgrades for the F-22 and F-35 to enhance overall combat effectiveness.
    paragraph_summary: The Air Force is transitioning to a three-tier air-dominance
      model, moving away from reliance on a single aircraft. Central to this strategy
      is the F-47 NGAD, designed as a deep-penetrating quarterback for contested environments,
      and intended to integrate with a broader system that includes loyal-wingman drones.
      Additionally, there are plans for a viability upgrade package to enhance existing
      aircraft capabilities, such as the F-22 and F-35, which will serve as enforcers
      and quarterbacks, respectively, in this new operational framework.

  - title: 'Forget the F-22 and F-35: China’s J-20 and J-35 Stealth Fighters Could Soon
      Have Double the Range'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/forget-the-f-22-and-f-35-chinas-j-20-and-j-35-stealth-fighters-could-soon-have-double-the-range/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – China’s airpower ambitions are expanding beyond
      stealth fighters to the support systems that make them truly strategic. -A new
      generation of aerial refueling tankers—most notably the Y-20U—is transforming
      the reach of Chinese aircraft such as the J-20 and carrier-borne J-35. -Refueling
      allows these fighters to stay aloft longer, strike farther […] The post Forget
      the F-22 and F-35: China’s J-20 and J-35 Stealth Fighters Could Soon Have Double
      the Range appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: China is enhancing its airpower capabilities by developing
      advanced aerial refueling tankers like the Y-20U, which significantly extend the
      operational range of its stealth fighters, the J-20 and J-35.
    paragraph_summary: China is significantly enhancing its airpower capabilities by
      not only developing advanced stealth fighters like the J-20 and J-35 but also
      by investing in crucial support systems such as a new generation of aerial refueling
      tankers, particularly the Y-20U. This strategic focus on refueling technology
      enables these fighters to extend their operational range and duration, allowing
      them to conduct missions further from their bases. As a result, China's air combat

      combat readiness in an evolving threat landscape.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/the-u-s-navy-is-one-giant-pressure-cooker-sailing-into-2026/
    text: Key points and Summary – Is the U.S. Navy in crisis? Not quite—but the strain
      is increasingly visible. -Procurement misfires like Zumwalt and LCS produced costly
      micro-fleets and early retirements, while constant concept churn signals uncertainty
      about what future naval warfare demands. -Aircraft carriers remain the centerpiece
      for power projection, yet China’s A2/AD environment is […] The post The U.S. Navy
      Is One Giant Pressure Cooker Sailing Into 2026 appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. Navy is facing increasing strain due to procurement
      issues and uncertainty in naval warfare concepts, while aircraft carriers continue
      to be central to power projection amid challenges posed by China's A2/AD environment.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the current state of the U.S. Navy, suggesting
      that while it is not in outright crisis, it is under increasing strain due to
      various challenges. Procurement issues, exemplified by projects like the Zumwalt
      and Littoral Combat Ship (LCS), have led to costly micro-fleets and premature
      retirements of vessels. Additionally, ongoing shifts in naval warfare concepts
      indicate uncertainty about future needs. Although aircraft carriers continue to
      play a crucial role in power projection, the growing anti-access/area denial (A2/AD)
      capabilities of China pose significant challenges. Overall, the Navy is likened
      to a pressure cooker, facing mounting pressures as it approaches 2026.

      presence. -Keeping those carriers relevant means targeted upgrades: modern landing

    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. Navy's reliance on Nimitz-class aircraft carriers
      for daily operations highlights the challenges posed by delays in the Ford-class
      ships and the need for targeted upgrades to maintain their relevance.
    paragraph_summary: The U.S. Navy is currently grappling with a dilemma regarding
      its aircraft carriers, particularly as delays in the Ford-class ships and backlogged
      shipyards leave the Nimitz-class carriers as the primary operational force for
      global presence. To maintain the relevance of the Nimitz-class, the Navy must
      implement targeted upgrades, including modern landing aids like JPALS, enhanced
      command-and-control systems, and improved integration with other military assets.
      This situation highlights that the challenges facing the Navy extend beyond just
      new technology; they also involve timely and effective modernization of existing
      capabilities.
